draft.title: Trade liberalisation in Australia
card: Trade liberalisation means cutting barriers to trade, such as tariffs. A tariff is a tax on imported goods that makes them dearer for buyers.
From the 1980s, Australia cut tariffs sharply. Protection for industries such as clothing, footwear and cars was reduced over time.
Lower tariffs expose local firms to competition from imports. Firms that cannot compete may shrink or close.
Resources such as labour and capital can then move to industries that produce at lower cost. This is a shift to more efficient uses, and it can lift productivity over time.
draft.remember: Cutting tariffs brings competition, and resources move to where they are used more efficiently.

a.q: Which of these is an example of trade liberalisation?
opts: The government cuts the tariff on imported clothing
The government lifts the tariff on imported clothing
The government pays a subsidy to local clothing firms
The government bans imports of some cheaper clothing
a.why: A lower tariff reduces a barrier to trade, which is liberalisation. A higher tariff, a ban and a subsidy to local firms all protect local industry, so they move the other way.
a.clue: Liberalisation means fewer barriers to trade.

b.q: Australia cuts the tariff on imported cars, and imported cars become cheaper. What is a likely effect on local car makers?
opts: They face more competition and some may close
They face less competition and can lift their prices
They gain, as buyers pay more for imported cars
They are unaffected, as buyers only want local cars
b.why: Cheaper imports give local makers more competition. Those that cannot match the cost or quality of imports may shrink or close. Less competition is wrong, because the tariff cut makes imports more attractive, not less.
b.clue: Think about what cheaper imports do for local buyers.

a.best: The government cuts the tariff on imported clothing
also_right: The government lifts the tariff on imported clothing

b.best: They face more competition and some may close

problems.detail: "Lifts the tariff" is ambiguous. The why reads it as raising the tariff, but in Australian usage "lifting" a tariff, like lifting a ban or sanctions, often means removing it, which would be liberalisation. A careful student could defend this option as right. Use "raises the tariff" instead.

proposal.title: Trade liberalisation in Australia
card: Protection shields local firms from imports, through tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on the amount imported) or subsidies to local firms. Trade liberalisation means reducing protection.
From the 1980s, Australia cut tariffs sharply and removed import quotas. Protection for industries such as clothing, footwear and cars was reduced over time.
Lower tariffs make imports cheaper and expose local firms to more competition. Firms that cannot compete may shrink or close.
Resources such as labour and capital can then move to industries that produce at lower cost. This is a shift to more efficient uses, and it can lift productivity over time.
proposal.remember: Cutting protection brings competition, and resources move to where they are used more efficiently.
